title: Grok Bot Is Here: What xAI's Always-On AI Agents Actually Do

blocks.text: Grok Bot Is Here: What xAI's Always-On AI Agents Actually Do

xAI launched Grok Bot on August 11, 2026: always-on AI agents that work on a cloud computer inside your real apps. Updated September 26, 2026 with current plans and pricing, plus four real use cases from launch-week walkthroughs.

Grok Bot is xAI's always-on AI agent product, launched in beta on August 11, 2026. Each Bot is a named agent with its own cloud computer that signs into your apps, finishes multi-step jobs and keeps working after you close the app. It is included on the Premium, Super and Ultra tiers of The X Subscription (from $30 a month) and on legacy Cursor paid plans.

xAI shipped Grok Bot on August 11, 2026: a beta product that gives you a roster of AI agents, called Bots, that work on a persistent cloud computer with a browser, file system and terminal. It is not a chat window. It is a set of coworkers you assign work to, and the work keeps running after you close your laptop.

Updated October 23, 2026: Cursor's pricing page now sells The X Subscription, and Cursor Pro, Pro+ and Ultra are now legacy plans. The pricing section and pricing FAQs were re-checked against cursor.com/pricing and cursor.com/help/grok-bot/plans that day. Everything else was checked September 26, 2026 against xAI's own pages (the August 11 launch post and the August 26 plans update) and Cursor's Grok Bot docs.

For anyone building or buying AI agents right now, Grok Bot is worth a close look, not because the idea is new (OpenClaw and Hermes have both tried variations of "an agent with its own computer"), but because of what shipped alongside it: a messenger-style interface regular people can actually operate on day one, a real mobile app, and a distribution deal through Cursor that puts it in front of a developer audience that already pays for AI tooling.
This breakdown is based on xAI's own launch material and hands-on walkthroughs recorded by independent creators the same week, with the actual product screens pulled directly from that footage.
What Is Grok Bot?

Grok Bot is xAI's always-on AI agent product, built on top of Grok and distributed jointly with Cursor. You sign in with a Cursor account, and Cursor's docs say the computers Bots work on run in Cursor's cloud. Each Bot you create gets:
A named role you assign it (email, LinkedIn outreach, research, scheduling)
Its own screen on a persistent cloud computer with a real browser, file system and terminal
Access to the logins you connect once, which your Bots reuse
Its own conversations and learned memory, kept separate from your other Bots
The ability to keep working after you close the app, because the work runs on a persistent cloud computer (optional local command execution on desktop)

One detail differs from most launch-week coverage. Per Cursor's Grok Bot docs, all of your Bots share one cloud computer per account, including its files, browser sessions and app logins. Each Bot gets its own screen on that computer, and one Bot runs one computer-use task on its screen at a time. Treat anything you put on that computer as visible to every Bot you run.

The cloud part is the actual product decision worth noticing. Most AI agent tools today, including well-known coding and research agents, run inside a chat window on your device. Grok Bot runs jobs in the cloud, then reports back. You can close your laptop mid-task and the Bot keeps going.

Availability (checked September 26, 2026): Grok Bot is still labeled beta. Cursor's docs list the desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux, and the mobile app for iPhone (iOS 18 or later, per the get started guide). Cursor's mobile help page says the mobile app is also on Android through Google Play. On August 26, 2026, xAI expanded access: Grok Bot is now included with SuperGrok, SuperGrok Plus, SuperGrok Heavy, Cursor Pro, Cursor Pro+, Cursor Ultra, and Cursor Teams Standard and Premium. See the pricing section below for what each plan costs and what is still unconfirmed.
Related Reads
Is Grok Bot the Same as @grok on X?

No. Searches for "grok bot" and "grok bots" often mean the @grok account on X, where you tag Grok in a reply. Grok Bot is a separate xAI product with its own apps, cloud computer and usage pool. This post covers Grok Bot only. xAI's Grok Bot pages do not document @grok, so we make no claims about how that account works or who can use it.

How Do You Set Up Grok Bot?

xAI's docs describe three steps. Create a Bot, describe its job in a message, then grant access to the tools it needs. There is no workflow builder to configure. Desktop apps exist for macOS, Windows and Linux, and mobile apps for iPhone, iPad and Android (docs.x.ai/grok-bot/overview, checked September 26, 2026). The docs also warn that some websites block automation or need a human to step in.
How Much Does Grok Bot Cost and Which Plans Include It?

Grok Bot has no separate subscription. Cursor's pricing page now sells The X Subscription, and Grok Bot is included on its Premium ($30 a month), Super ($100) and Ultra ($200) tiers, plus every paid seat on a Teams plan (from $30 per user a month). It is not included on Free or Plus ($8). On these plans Grok Bot draws from one shared weekly pool with Cursor and the Grok apps, and Super and Ultra get larger pools than Premium.

Earlier subscribers keep access. Cursor's help page now calls Cursor Pro, Pro+, Ultra and the self-serve Teams plan legacy plans, and all of them still include Grok Bot with a weekly allowance. On a legacy Cursor account, a linked SuperGrok, SuperGrok Plus, SuperGrok Heavy or X Premium+ subscription, or a seat on a self-serve Grok Business plan, also grants access.
What is confirmed on those pages:

Free trial. Cursor's help page says the Grok Bot free trial is a usage credit, measured by agent steps and tokens, with a 7-day window. A single long job can use most or all of it, and used credit is not restored.

Extra usage. On The X Subscription, usage past the weekly pool is paid from prepaid credit: buy credit, turn on Auto Top-up and set a monthly limit at grok.com/dashboard/billing. On legacy Cursor plans, work can continue as on-demand usage billed through Cursor if on-demand is enabled.
Plans do not stack. A legacy Cursor plan and a SuperGrok or X Premium+ link do not add together. Grok Bot uses whichever grants more weekly usage. Links are not part of The X Subscription.

Team plans. On a team on The X Subscription, every paid seat includes Grok Bot. On a legacy self-serve Cursor Teams plan, every member has access with no Premium seat required. Enterprise access goes through your account executive.

What we could not confirm: SuperGrok, SuperGrok Plus, SuperGrok Heavy and X Premium+ prices, the exact size of any weekly pool (none of these pages give a number), and the date The X Subscription replaced Cursor's Pro, Pro+ and Ultra lineup.
How Do You Use Grok Bot?

Opening the desktop app looks closer to iMessage than to a typical AI chat product. Every conversation centers on Bots, not tasks. A walkthrough recorded the week of launch shows a sidebar of named Bots, each with a distinct role: one for email, one for LinkedIn research, one for negotiating deals, one for general use.

You are not limited to one Bot per conversation either. You can put several Bots in a group chat, and xAI's launch post says they can message each other, pass work and assign ownership on their own. The product is explicitly asking you to think in terms of roles, not tasks: instead of "summarize this document," you are building a team member who handles a category of work indefinitely.

Setting up a new Bot does not involve a settings panel. You describe what you want in plain language ("I need help planning a vacation and finding the best flight deal"), and the Bot asks clarifying questions, drafts a plan, and starts working. It will even name and describe itself if you ask it to.

One detail matters more than it looks: Grok Bot does not let you pick which underlying model runs a given task. Cursor's settings docs say it directly: "Cursor manages model selection, so there's no model picker." For most users that is a convenience. For technical teams evaluating this for real workflows, the lack of a model-selection or advanced mode is a real limitation worth flagging before you commit a team to it.
Handing Over Control for Logins
Because Bots work on a cloud computer, some tasks require you to log in on their behalf, once, so they can keep working without you pasting credentials into chat.

When a Bot needs LinkedIn access to research companies, it navigates to the login screen itself and hands control back to you with a "sign in, then hand it back" prompt. You authenticate, click done, and the Bot resumes from where you left it. This pattern, watch the Bot get most of the way there and step in only for the sensitive part, is the same trust model used for connecting Notion, Gmail, and Google Drive. Cursor's docs add that for supported connections a masked secret field keeps the value out of the transcript and away from the model, and that you should never paste passwords or one-time codes into ordinary chat.
Beyond manual handoff, Grok Bot ships with a plugin library for the integrations it expects teams to use most:

Notion, Slack, Google Drive, AWS Agents, AWS SageMaker, Browserbase, Composio, and Context7 all showed up as one-click connections in the launch-week footage, alongside an option to build a custom plugin. Bots use plugins where available (faster, more reliable) and computer use for everything else (more flexible, works with sites that have no API). You are not expected to configure this yourself; it surfaces the connection prompt only when a task actually needs it.
Teaching a Bot a New Workflow by Recording It
The feature most relevant to actual businesses evaluating AI agent development is the "teach a task" mode.

Clicking teach a task puts the Bot into a recording state on its own screen. You walk through a workflow step by step, open this site, click here, fill this field, and the Bot turns the demonstration into a draft skill it can repeat. Combined with routines (recurring, scheduled runs of a task a Bot already knows how to do), this is the closest thing in Grok Bot to a no-code automation builder: instead of describing a workflow in words, you perform it once and the Bot generalizes from the demonstration.

Two current details from Cursor's docs: teach a task is rolling out gradually, so the button may not show up for you yet (you can ask the Bot to build a skill from written instructions instead), and a single Bot can own up to 50 routines.

This matters for the same reason robotic process automation mattered a decade ago: the bottleneck for automating a workflow is rarely the technology, it is the time it takes someone to specify the workflow precisely enough for software to execute it reliably. A screen recording removes most of that specification cost.
Desktop and Mobile Are the Same Product

The mobile app is not a stripped-down companion. Cursor's docs say the iPhone app connects to the same Bots, conversations, routines, and cloud computer as desktop, and the launch-week footage shows the live view of a Bot's screen on the phone, including the ability to take over a Bot's session. In the same walkthrough, the reviewer's actual Bot roster illustrates the role-based pattern well: a browser agent, a LinkedIn outreach agent, a research agent, an email assistant, a scripting agent, and a general-purpose Grok chat, all addressable from a single phone screen.

That parity is a distribution decision as much as an engineering one. A tool you can only fully use at a desk gets checked once a day. A tool with full parity on the device already in your pocket gets checked, and used to assign new work, throughout the day.

Real Use Cases People Are Already Running

A second hands-on breakdown, recorded the same week as launch, walks through four Bots the reviewer actually put to work rather than just demoed. The pattern across all four is the same: describe the outcome once, let the Bot figure out the mechanism.

Recurring reporting from a demonstration, not an integration. One Bot was taught to pull newsletter post statistics from Beehiiv purely by watching a single screen recording of the reviewer doing it manually. No API, no plugin for that specific report. The Bot turned the recording into a repeatable skill and now runs the same statistics pull on request.

Social monitoring on a schedule. A second Bot was told, in one sentence, to watch a specific X account and message the reviewer whenever a new post appeared. It built its own 30-minute checking routine using the browser, with no manual scheduling step required.

Inbox triage through a plugin instead of a screen. A third Bot connected to Gmail through an MCP plugin (an OAuth-style connection, not a screen recording) and started pulling and summarizing emails immediately, since that specific task already had a reliable integration available.

Account research using full computer access, not just a browser tab. In the same walkthrough, a Bot was pointed at a Salesforce account and left to log in and navigate the CRM itself, the way a person would, rather than calling a Salesforce API. The reviewer's own framing is worth repeating directly: an estimated 80 percent of the internet has no API or MCP a Bot could call instead, which is exactly the gap full computer access is built to cover.

None of these four are exotic. That is the point. Reporting, monitoring, inbox triage, and CRM research are the same tasks most operations teams already run manually, and each one picked a different mechanism, screen recording, scheduled browser routine, plugin, or full computer control, based on what the specific tool actually supported. xAI's own examples point the same way: its August 26 post lists Bots working as a sales prospector, website builder, inbox manager, customer support agent and meeting stand-in.
Grok Bot vs a Typical AI Chat Agent
What Are Grok Bot's Limits?
Three limitations stand out:
No model control. There is no way to choose or constrain which model handles a task, which matters for teams with compliance, cost, or reliability requirements around specific model behavior.

No live voice mode. In the launch-week walkthroughs, the only voice input was dictation into a text field. A live, conversational mode, where you talk through several tasks and have them assigned to different Bots in real time, was not available.

Usage, not price, is now the gate. The entry point is now the $30 Premium tier of The X Subscription, and each plan comes with a weekly pool that none of the official pages size in numbers. Heavy agent jobs burn through it and then move to paid extra usage. Set the monthly additional usage limit before you hand a Bot anything long.
What This Means If You're Evaluating AI Agents for Your Business

The specific product matters less than the pattern it validates: agents that own a persistent environment (their own computer, their own logins, their own memory of what they have already done) are outperforming agents that only exist inside a chat turn. That is the same architectural direction we build toward with clients through custom AI agent development: role-scoped agents with their own credentials and their own state, coordinated rather than crammed into a single do-everything assistant.

If your team is evaluating whether an off-the-shelf tool like Grok Bot fits, or whether the workflow is specific enough to warrant a custom build, the deciding factor is usually the same one that shows up in Grok Bot's own gaps: does the task need a specific model, a specific compliance boundary, or integration with an internal tool that has no public plugin? Off-the-shelf agent products are built for breadth. Custom agent builds exist for the workflows breadth does not reach.

FAQ
What is Grok Bot?

Grok Bot is xAI's always-on AI agent product, launched in beta on August 11, 2026. You create named Bots, give each a role, and they work on a persistent cloud computer with a browser, file system and terminal, so work continues after you close your device. It is distributed jointly with Cursor and uses your Cursor account.
Is Grok Bot free?

Not as an ongoing plan. Cursor's help page describes a free trial given as a usage credit, measured by agent steps and tokens, with a 7-day window. After that you need Premium, Super or Ultra on The X Subscription, a legacy Cursor plan (Pro, Pro+, Ultra or Teams), or a linked SuperGrok or X Premium+ account. The Free and Plus tiers of The X Subscription do not include Grok Bot.
Which plans include Grok Bot?

As of October 23, 2026, Cursor's help page lists Premium, Super and Ultra on The X Subscription (individual and team seats), legacy Cursor Pro, Pro+, Ultra and Teams, linked SuperGrok, SuperGrok Plus, SuperGrok Heavy or X Premium+ accounts, and seats on a self-serve Grok Business plan. Free and Plus on The X Subscription do not include it. SuperGrok Lite, SuperGrok Team and SuperGrok Enterprise cannot link. Cursor Enterprise access goes through your account executive.
How much does Grok Bot cost?

Grok Bot has no separate subscription. On Cursor's pricing page (October 23, 2026), it is included from the Premium tier of The X Subscription at $30 a month, then Super at $100 and Ultra at $200, with Teams from $30 per user. Plus ($8) and Free do not include it. Legacy Cursor Pro, Pro+ and Ultra plans still include it. Extra usage past the weekly pool is paid from prepaid credit.
Is Grok Bot the same as @grok on X?

No. Grok Bot is xAI's agent product with its own apps and cloud computer. The @grok account on X is a different way to reach Grok. xAI's Grok Bot pages do not cover @grok, so check X's own help pages for how it works.
How do I set up Grok Bot?

Per xAI's docs, create a Bot, describe its job in a message, then grant it access to the tools it needs. Install the desktop app or the mobile app and sign in with your Cursor account. Some websites block automation or ask you to step in.
What devices does Grok Bot run on?

xAI's docs list desktop apps for macOS, Windows and Linux, and mobile apps for iPhone, iPad and Android. Everything runs on a cloud computer, so work continues when your device is off. Docs checked September 26, 2026 at docs.x.ai/grok-bot/overview.
How is Grok Bot different from Grok chat?

Grok chat answers you inside a conversation. Grok Bot runs agents on a cloud computer that sign into your apps, do multi-step work in the real tools, and keep going when you close the app. On The X Subscription, Grok Bot draws from the same weekly pool as Cursor and the Grok apps, so long Bot jobs do eat into your chat and coding usage. On legacy Cursor plans and linked accounts, Grok Bot has its own weekly allowance.
Is Grok Bot available on Android?

Yes. As of September 26, 2026, Cursor's Grok Bot mobile help page says the app is available on iOS and Android, installed from the App Store or Google Play. You sign in with the same Cursor account and get the same cloud computer as on desktop. The desktop app runs on macOS, Windows and Linux.
How is Grok Bot different from a regular AI chatbot?

A regular AI chatbot produces its output inside the chat window and stops working when you close it. Grok Bot's agents run on a cloud computer, keep working when your device is off, and produce output directly inside the tool being used (an inbox, a CRM, a document) rather than in the chat.
Can I choose which AI model Grok Bot uses for a task?
No. Cursor's Grok Bot settings docs say Cursor manages model selection and there is no model picker. This is a limitation for technical teams with specific model requirements.
What is the "teach a task" feature in Grok Bot?

Teach a task puts a Bot into a recording mode where you demonstrate a browser workflow step by step. The Bot turns the recording into a draft skill it can repeat, including on a schedule through routines. Cursor's docs say the feature is rolling out gradually, so it may not appear on every account yet.
Should a business build a custom AI agent instead of using Grok Bot?

It depends on the workflow. Off-the-shelf tools like Grok Bot are built for breadth across common tasks. A workflow with specific compliance, model, or internal-tool requirements that Grok Bot cannot meet is a better fit for custom AI agent development.
